v.why: Raising an already high learning rate causes divergence and large accuracy drops on all datasets (experiments 3, 5, 17, 18, 20).
With very small learning rates the network is undertrained in 243 epochs, so increasing the rate helps (experiments 2, 4, 14).
Raising an already strong L2 penalty causes heavy underfitting (experiments 84, 94-97, 100).
At tiny alpha values, one more step of regularization is negligible or slightly helpful, unlike at large alpha (experiment 82 vs 84).
Larger batches reduce gradient noise and partially stabilize training at high learning rates (experiments 25, 27, 35).
Wider networks are more prone to instability at high learning rates (experiments 45, 59).
Deeper networks diverge more easily at high learning rates (experiments 64, 65).
At low learning rates, extra depth adds useful capacity without causing instability (experiments 63, 66, 80).
Narrow networks are capacity-limited, so adding units helps more than it does for already wide ones (experiments 53, 54, 56 vs 43).
At large batch sizes, a further increase cuts the number of updates per epoch and hurts convergence (experiment 36).

raw:
Most of these hypotheses rest on a few patterns in the 100 experiments:

- **Learning rate:** raising it is badly destabilizing once it is already high (0.0215 or above), but helps when it is very low.
- **L2 penalty:** raising alpha is very damaging when it is already large (0.0167 or above), but close to neutral when it is small.
- **Larger capacity at high learning rate:** adding width or depth hurts more when the learning rate is high. Adding depth helps when the learning rate is low, likely because the network is undertrained.
- **Batch size:** a larger batch partly rescues runs with a high learning rate. At the largest batch sizes it hurts, because there are fewer updates.
- **Width:** adding units helps most when the network starts narrow.

Two hypotheses are weaker than the rest:

- **Width up at low width (#9):** this rests on only three experiments (#53, #54, #56), and two of them have a negative result on one dataset.
- **Batch size up at large batch (#10):** this mostly comes from one clearly negative case (#36), and #23 and #37 disagree across datasets.
